claims.text: Alloying PGM nanoparticles with non-PGM transition metals can create atomically isolated PGM active sites.
Alloying PGM and non-PGM atoms modulates the electronic structure of the PGM sites.
The electronic modulation specifically shifts the d-band center of isolated PGM sites.
The baseline pure-PGM or Pt-based nanoparticles have a conventional d-band profile and lack isolated active sites.
Introducing a controlled concentration of Cu or a similar non-PGM dopant will form a multimetal alloy containing isolated PGM sites.
The isolated PGM centers are embedded in a non-PGM-containing matrix.
The isolated active sites are characterized by a broadened, featureless valence-band spectrum.
Synergistic electronic interactions and charge transfer occur between the PGM and non-PGM components.
Electronic-structure modulation tunes the adsorption strength of catalytic reaction intermediates.
The modified electronic structure optimizes adsorption and oxidation of ethanol intermediates.
Optimized adsorption and desorption suppresses poisoning by strongly adsorbed CO-like intermediates.
The isolated-site electronic structure facilitates complete ethanol oxidation through its multistep 12-electron and 12-proton pathway.
The modified catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential and a higher current density than the undoped baseline.
The modified catalyst will favor complete ethanol-oxidation products over partial-oxidation byproducts.
The modified catalyst will exhibit improved durability during extended electrochemical cycling.
High potentials, strongly oxidizing conditions, or irreversible surface passivation can erase the alloy-induced d-band modulation and diminish the catalytic benefits.
